claims: Artemis II will follow a ~10-day, figure-eight path.
Artemis II will launch from Kennedy Space Center (FL).
Artemis II will conduct a crewed flyby of the Moon.
Artemis II will return to a Pacific Ocean splashdown.
Orion spacecraft will perform initial Earth orbits for systems checks.
Orion spacecraft will use a free-return trajectory.
The free-return trajectory loops around the far side of the Moon roughly 3,000–9,000 miles above the surface.
The free-return trajectory will slingshot back to Earth.
Space Launch System (SLS) rocket lifts off from Kennedy Space Center (FL).
Space Launch System (SLS) rocket sends Orion into an initial high-Earth orbit to check systems.
A burn from the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS) will propel the crew toward the Moon.
Orion will pass behind the far side of the Moon.
Orion will use the Moon's gravity to assist in a free-return loop back toward Earth.
The service module will separate from the crew module before atmospheric re-entry.
The launch is designed to be visible from parts of Florida, Georgia, and the surrounding region within the first 70 seconds.
Artemis II is currently planned for 2026.
Artemis II will be the first crewed flight to leave low Earth orbit since 1972.
